blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Large-scale change almost always takes longer and costs more than its sponsors initially believe. That is not a failure of planning; it is a structural feature of organisations in which momentum, politics and habit combine to resist any meaningful shift. Leaders who understand this early suffer less and succeed more than those who discover it gradually through disappointment.

What works, more often than not, is a small number of clearly articulated commitments, repeated relentlessly for at least eighteen months. The temptation is always to add more — more themes, more initiatives, more announcements — but the leaders who actually move large organisations tend to say the same three things in slightly different words for a year and a half. By the end, those three things have penetrated all the way to the edges of the business, and the change has become, quietly, the new default.

Were a leader to focus only on the rational case for change — the strategic logic, the commercial benefits, the competitive necessity — the change would, in most organisations, simply not happen. The emotional and psychological work is what finally shifts behaviour, and it is work that cannot be delegated. Senior leaders who understand this do not merely sponsor transformation; they inhabit it publicly, personally and sometimes uncomfortably.

items.q: According to the text, why does large-scale change take longer and cost more than expected?
options: Because planning is almost always done badly
Because competitors interfere with the process
Because it is a structural feature of organisations that resist meaningful shifts
Because sponsors deliberately understate the budget
items.why: "it is a structural feature of organisations in which momentum, politics and habit combine to resist any meaningful shift" — não é falha de planejamento.

items.q: What does the text say actually works in moving large organisations?
options: Launching as many initiatives as possible at once
Delegating the change to middle managers
Replacing the senior leadership team
A small number of commitments repeated relentlessly for at least eighteen months
items.why: "a small number of clearly articulated commitments, repeated relentlessly for at least eighteen months."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Emotional work is essential to shifting behaviour
Repetition is more powerful than novelty in large-scale change
The strongest change programmes keep adding new themes to stay fresh
Leaders should expect resistance as a structural feature
items.why: Inferência: o texto argumenta contra acrescentar mais temas — "The temptation is always to add more… but".

items.q: What does the sentence beginning "Were a leader to focus only on the rational case…" suggest?
options: Commercial benefits are irrelevant to transformation
Logic alone is enough to secure change
Relying solely on logic would usually cause the change to fail
The strategic case should be hidden from staff
items.why: Inferência: a hipótese condicional indica que só a lógica "would… simply not happen" — a mudança não aconteceria.

items.q: What is implied by the phrase "they inhabit it publicly, personally and sometimes uncomfortably"?
options: Genuine transformation requires visible personal exposure, not just formal endorsement
Sponsorship is all that senior leaders need to provide
Leaders must move their offices during the change
Discomfort is a sign the strategy is wrong
items.why: Inferência: "do not merely sponsor… they inhabit it" — a mudança exige envolvimento pessoal e exposto, além do aval formal.

blocks.instruction: Ouça James falando com a equipe durante a transformação. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
So I've just come out of the São Paulo session, and it's the fourth country this month. I'll be honest with you — I stood there and I nearly added a fourth priority to the slide, because someone asked a very reasonable question about the supply chain, and my instinct was to promise them something.

And then I stopped. Because if I add a fourth thing here, I'll add a fifth in Singapore, and by the time we reach the smaller offices, nobody will remember what we actually stand for. So I bit my tongue and I said the same three sentences I've said in every room for the last nine months.

The strange part is what happens when you repeat yourself that many times. In the early weeks it felt almost embarrassing — people were clearly thinking, yes, you've told us this before. But somewhere around month six, they started finishing my sentences for me. The words had stopped being mine. They'd become theirs.

We're only halfway. Nine more months of saying the same three things. It is not glamorous work, and honestly it can be lonely. But this is the part I refuse to hand to anyone else.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: Why did James nearly add a fourth priority during the São Paulo session?
options: Someone asked a reasonable question and his instinct was to promise something
He had forgotten one of the original three
The three priorities had already been achieved
The board instructed him to expand the plan
items.why: "someone asked a very reasonable question about the supply chain, and my instinct was to promise them something."

items.q: What did James do instead of adding the fourth priority?
options: He removed one of the existing priorities
He asked the audience to vote on it
He repeated the same three sentences he'd used in every room
He postponed the session to the next day
items.why: "I bit my tongue and I said the same three sentences I've said in every room for the last nine months."

items.q: What happened around month six, according to James?
options: He decided to change the three priorities
People started finishing his sentences for him
The smaller offices were closed
The programme was quietly cancelled
items.why: "somewhere around month six, they started finishing my sentences for me."

items.q: What does James mean when he says "The words had stopped being mine. They'd become theirs."?
options: The staff were quoting him without permission
The commitments had been internalised by the organisation
Other leaders had rewritten his speech
He had lost control of the message
items.why: Inferência: a repetição fez as ideias serem absorvidas — deixaram de ser dele e passaram a ser da própria equipe.

items.q: What can be inferred about James's view of his own role in the change?
options: He plans to hand the message over to the regional offices soon
He sees the repetitive work as essential and refuses to delegate it, despite the discomfort
He finds the work glamorous and enjoys the attention
He believes the change is already complete
items.why: Inferência: "It is not glamorous work… it can be lonely. But this is the part I refuse to hand to anyone else."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "The programme survived because of the CEO's strategic patience." Strategic patience means…
options: the willingness to hold a course over the long term rather than chase quick wins
a tolerance for missed deadlines
the ability to delegate difficult decisions
a detailed project timeline
items.why: Strategic patience = paciência estratégica: manter o rumo no longo prazo, sem ceder à pressa por resultados rápidos.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "Even a brilliant plan stalls when it meets the ___ of a large, slow-moving company."
options: narrative discipline
organisational inertia
sponsorship
behavioural shift
items.why: Organisational inertia = inércia organizacional: a resistência estrutural ao movimento.

items.q: "After a dozen competing announcements, the staff showed clear signs of change fatigue." This refers to…
options: physical exhaustion from overtime
confusion about the company's finances
enthusiasm for a fresh initiative
weariness and disengagement caused by too many change messages
items.why: Change fatigue = fadiga de mudança: o cansaço que vem do excesso de mensagens, não da falta delas.

items.q: Narrative discipline is best described as…
options: the discipline of repeating a small, consistent story rather than adding new messages
keeping strict records of every meeting
writing a detailed annual report
punishing employees who resist change
items.why: Narrative discipline = disciplina narrativa: manter poucas mensagens consistentes, resistindo à tentação de somar novas.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "A memo signals intent, but only a real ___ proves the culture has actually moved."
options: behavioural shift
transformation
edge of the business
sponsorship
items.why: Behavioural shift = mudança de comportamento: a prova concreta de que a cultura mudou de fato.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em reuniões de transformação. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "None of these announcements will move the needle unless people change how they work." To move the needle means to…
options: make a noticeable, measurable difference
create internal resistance
restart the project
delay the decision
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, produzir diferença perceptível e mensurável.

items.q: "We agreed the vision, but nobody followed through once the pressure eased." They…
options: failed to carry the plan to completion
carried the plan to completion
documented the plan carefully
rewrote the plan from scratch
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado; aqui, justamente o que não aconteceu.

items.q: "The board finally signed off on the eighteen-month timeline." To sign off on means to…
options: comment informally
postpone indefinitely
quietly ignore
formally approve
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "Several country heads pushed back on the idea of repeating the same three messages." They…
options: forgot about it
implemented it in secret
approved it immediately
resisted or challenged the idea
items.why: Push back on = resistir, contestar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "We must stay the course even when the early results look flat." To stay the course means to…
options: abandon the plan and try something new
speed up the timeline dramatically
continue with the chosen strategy despite difficulty
hand the plan to another team
items.why: Stay the course = manter o rumo, persistir na estratégia escolhida apesar das dificuldades.
